text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London closed marginally higher in quiet trade. August added 50 cents to close at $321.70 per tonne, while October rose by $1.1 to close at $317.40 per tonne. Brazil's key port Santos was partially paralysed by an indefinite strike involving a group of administrative workers. Some 23 ships docked in CODESP berths have been hit by the strike, including 8 ships loading bagged sugar and one loading bulk sugar. However, this remained without influence on world market prices.

Raw sugar futures in New York ended higher but off the day's highs after early buying failed to attract follow- through. October added 5 points to close at 11.24 cents/lb, while March closed 8 points higher at 11.31 cents/lb. Trade sources expect range bound and thin dealings ahead of the independence day holiday on Friday. However, the low level of physical offtake will sooner or later weigh on prices.

E.D.& F. MAN - World sugar production 1996/97 (October/September) will total 122.96 million tonnes, down from 123.71 million tonnes the previous year, according to a report released by international trade house E.D.& F. Man. This compares with our latest September/August year figures (June 19) of 123.16 and 125.86 million tonnes respectively. Consumption in October/September 1996/97 is put at 120.71 million tonnes, up from 118.58 million tonnes the previous year also roughly in line with our own projections.

Man said preliminary figures support the view of a potentially tighter market in 1997/98. It was added that much of this outlook depends on the premise that the world's largest producer, India, will have a significantly lower crop. Current indications suggest that this will be the case with planted area expected to be significantly lower due to widespread farmer dissatisfaction because of late payment for their cane, Man said.

This will have serious consequences for the raws whites mix. Man emphasized that with the Middle East refineries getting fully under way, raws will be in greater demand at the expense of whites that will be struggling to find homes. The prospect of India potentially returning as a large net importer next season has rather distorted this scenario and put the pressure back on the whites, Man said. However, with Brazil effectively having the ability to switch its large availability of interchangeable crystals from raws to whites, as and when one of the other becomes more economically attractive, any developing imbalance can be alleviated almost single-handedly by the world's leading exporter, it was added.

There has recently been talk of a pending white sugar shortage before new crop sugars come onto the market. However, this was probably more wishful thinking than anything else and Man said in its latest market report that the paucity of white sugar offtake has restricted export avenues. It was added that this is not only hindering the prospects of East and Central European export opportunities but it is reflected in the trickle of EU exports. It was added that currently stock holdings in many of the EU countries are higher than normal, and with the present tender series due to end in six weeks time, the Commission may not achieve its planned export programme.

PAKISTAN - Meteorologists in Pakistan warned the Ministry of Food, Agriculture and Livestock that Pakistan's sugar cane crop this season could be affected by a fast-developing El Nino weather pattern over the Pacific Ocean. The consequence may be less monsoon rains, which might reduce the country's water reservoirs, which in turn could badly affect sugar cane production. The sugar cane crop needs water particularly between July and September, the key monsoon season.

EUROPE - There were again abundant rains in Western Europe's sugar beet areas (25-75 mm) during the week ended July 1. The only area where the rainfall was welcomed was in eastern Germany where it had been previously too dry. So far the rains do not pose any problems but further heavy rains could increase the risk of disease damage. In Italy, light to moderate (5-22 mm) rainfall occurred during the period under review. June rainfall was approximately 75 per cent of normal. Soil moisture supplies are slightly below normal, but prospects are stable. In Spain rainfall was light, but crop conditions are stable and soil moisture is adequate.

In Eastern Europe increased rainfall improved crop prospects in Poland. Near normal rainfall amounts were observed elsewhere. Most of southeastern Europe is in very good condition and Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria expect a good crop. In the beet growing areas of the former Soviet Union rainfall was light. Latest information from the Russian Federation suggests that the harvested area this year will not be more than 944,000 ha, down from 1.071 million ha the previous year. Soil moisture is adequate for favourable vegetative growth across the belt.
